implemented_requirements.evidence: reversi.py: self.board = [[EMPTY] * 8 for _ in range(8)] and the four central squares are set to WHITE/B​LACK.
reversi.py: self.current = BLACK; pass_turn() switches current via opponent_of(). main.py calls game.pass_turn() after each move and when a player has no valid moves.
reversi.py: valid_moves() builds a set using flips_for() for each empty cell; flips_for() returns a list of discs that would be flipped.

implemented_requirements.requirement: Flipping opponent discs when a move is applied
implemented_requirements.evidence: reversi.py: apply_move() calls flips_for(), places the piece, then iterates over flips and sets board[r][c] = player.

implemented_requirements.requirement: Game ends when board is full or no valid moves remain
implemented_requirements.evidence: reversi.py: game_over() returns True when both valid_moves(BLACK) and valid_moves(WHITE) are empty, which also covers a full board.
reversi.py: score() counts B and W pieces; main.py and render() print the scores after each turn and at game over.
main.py: parse_move() accepts "row col" or algebraic notation like "d3" and returns (row, col) indices.

implemented_requirements.requirement: Console UI showing board and prompting players
implemented_requirements.evidence: main.py: render() builds a textual board; main() prints it each loop and asks for input.

judge.summary: The provided files contain a complete, runnable Reversi implementation. Core game mechanics—board setup, turn alternation, move validation, disc flipping, end‑game detection, and scoring—are all present and demonstrably coded. The console interface parses common move formats and displays the board and scores. No missing functionality or fatal bugs are evident, so the submission meets the benchmark requirements.
